questions.prompt: A manager inherits a list where every current project stays active and one new priority is added at the top. Which response best fits priority discipline?
choices: She should rank the full list again so the new item has a clearer place.
She should ask each project owner to report progress more often until the list settles.
She should name which lower-value work will stop or wait so attention is freed.
questions.explanation: The source fact says priorities need posteriorities. A better ranking is not enough if every commitment keeps its claim.

questions.prompt: You have three major projects open and none has enough attention to finish. What would concentration change first?
choices: You would keep all three moving so ambition stays visible across the whole list.
You would give one major task enough sustained attention to reach completion.
You would split each project into smaller pieces so switching feels less costly.
questions.explanation: Concentration means one major task gets enough attention to finish. Many underpowered efforts are the common error.

questions.prompt: A team keeps funding an old report because it once helped senior leaders make decisions. Which reading matches planned abandonment?
choices: Past usefulness should be tested against current contribution before the report keeps resources.
Past usefulness should protect the report unless a replacement is already popular.
Past usefulness should earn the report a smaller budget while the same routine continues.
questions.explanation: Yesterday's success can become a trap. Reputation and habit do not prove the work still deserves resources.

questions.prompt: An urgent meeting request arrives while your main project has its only clear work block. What should you test before accepting?
choices: You should ask what result the request serves and what priority it would displace.
You should accept because urgency usually signals the work with the highest value.
You should decline when the request seems to carry another person's agenda.
questions.explanation: Urgency is not a reliable guide to importance. The useful test is contribution and displacement, not volume.

questions.prompt: A director hears the word abandonment and worries it means admitting defeat. Which answer keeps planned abandonment intact?
choices: Abandonment should be delayed until a project has no defenders left.
Abandonment can create capacity by releasing people, money, and attention.
Abandonment mainly works as a morale signal that a new era has begun.
questions.explanation: Planned abandonment is part of priority discipline because it frees capacity. It is not mainly a failure sign.

questions.prompt: A planner says the Bell System was large enough that focus would arise on its own. Which correction follows the source case?
choices: A large network can rely on scale because operating demands naturally align.
A large network should add more local priorities so each group feels represented.
A large network needs disciplined choices because daily demands can fragment attention.
questions.explanation: The Bell System example supports priority over scattered operating demands. Scale can increase fragmentation unless choices are disciplined.

questions.prompt: A trainee treats Vail's AT&T priority as a scheduling preference. What does the case actually illustrate?
choices: A governing service idea can filter competing opportunities against a central result.
A leader's calendar habits can make any activity feel more orderly to the staff.
A strict schedule can prevent new opportunities from disturbing daily routines.
questions.explanation: Vail illustrates purpose as a filter for choices. The priority is anchored in service, not personal calendar taste.

questions.prompt: You find six useful tasks in the same afternoon and want to pursue them all now. What does scarcity require you to admit?
choices: Useful tasks should each receive a small share so no good option is neglected.
Useful tasks become priorities once they can be described in concrete terms.
Useful tasks still compete for the same limited attention and capacity.
questions.explanation: Usefulness alone does not establish priority. Scarcity means worthwhile tasks compete for the same limited resources.

questions.prompt: A team refuses to revisit a chosen priority because changing it may look inconsistent. Which response fits planned abandonment?
choices: The team should preserve the priority until every promised milestone is complete.
The team should review it when conditions change because persistence can protect obsolete work.
The team should replace it quickly so people see that priorities remain flexible.
questions.explanation: Priority decisions need review when conditions change. Sticking with obsolete work can protect yesterday at tomorrow's expense.

reviewCards.front: Why is a priority list incomplete until it names posteriorities?
reviewCards.back: A priority list only shows the desired order. Posteriorities show what stops, waits, or loses resources so the first priority has real attention behind it.

reviewCards.front: What does concentration require beyond caring about important work?
reviewCards.back: It requires giving one major task enough sustained attention to finish. Caring about many important projects at once can still leave them all underpowered.

reviewCards.front: How can yesterday's success become a resource trap?
reviewCards.back: An old activity can keep money, people, and meetings because it once mattered. Planned abandonment asks whether it still contributes enough to deserve them.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate learned effectiveness (Ch 1), then use it on this priority problem?
reviewCards.back: Learned effectiveness turns responsibility into repeatable habits that produce useful results. Here, the habit is naming what stops so attention reaches the work that matters.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Bell System case warn against trusting scale to create focus?
reviewCards.back: A large technical network has more daily demands, not automatic coherence. Disciplined priorities keep operating pressure from fragmenting institutional attention.

reviewCards.front: What does Vail add to priority setting that a calendar cannot supply?
reviewCards.back: Vail's service idea gives choices a governing purpose. The filter is contribution to telephone service, not which task fits neatly on the schedule.

implementationPlan.title: Name the Stop
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Name the Stop by pairing every priority with the work that will stop, wait, or lose resources. The skill keeps concentration honest. You are not choosing first things until a lower-value claim has actually been deprived.

ifThenPlans.context: A new priority is added while the old list stays untouched.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a priority is added, then Name the Stop by writing the project, meeting, or request that will pause to fund it.

ifThenPlans.context: An old activity asks for renewal because it once worked.
ifThenPlans.plan: If old success asks for fresh resources, then Name the Stop by asking what current contribution would justify keeping it.

ifThenPlans.context: A loud request tries to take your best attention.
ifThenPlans.plan: If urgency presses in, then Name the Stop by asking what priority the request would displace before you answer.

ifThenPlans.context: Several useful tasks all look worth doing now.
ifThenPlans.plan: If everything looks useful, then Name the Stop by choosing one major effort and naming the useful work that will wait.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, pre-write one reply for the moment a new request crowds your priority: "I can consider this if we stop or delay ___." Move that draft beside the artifact you check most.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For each workday this week, keep a three-column Stop Log: first priority, named stop, resource freed. At the end, circle the day when the stop created the clearest attention.

memorableLines.text: A priority without a posteriority is a wish.
memorableLines.why: It makes the chapter's hard edge portable.

memorableLines.text: Pressure shouts; purpose sorts.
memorableLines.why: It separates urgency from contribution in five words.

memorableLines.text: Posteriorities are the proof of priorities.
memorableLines.why: It states the practical test of concentration.

chapters.title: The Elements of Decision-making
chapters.hook: 2 of the 5 decision elements start after agreement, where many bad choices quietly fail.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like delay is actually speed insurance. A decision gets faster when you first name the kind of problem, the result it must meet, and the person who will act.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff, touch your laptop lid and add one tick beside the choice if it names the owner, date, and first feedback check.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Decide by running the elements in order: classify the problem, name the must-meet result, choose the right answer, assign action, and check reality.

breakdown.fastRead:
A missed file sits in the upload queue, and everyone can name the meeting where it was approved. No one can name who owned the next step. That is how many decisions fail: not in the vote, but in the blank space after it.

You need more than a good opinion. You need decision elements, a short set of checks that turn a choice into work people can do. First ask what kind of problem this is. Then name the result any answer must meet before anyone starts bargaining. Compromise is safest after the right answer is plain.

Agreement is not the finish line. An unassigned decision is only a wish. The last test is feedback: what did you expect to happen, and what did the world do instead?
breakdown.deepRead:
Your meeting can fool itself in several ways. Classification stops you from treating a recurring problem like a surprise. The must-meet result keeps preference from taking over. The right answer gives you a standard before compromise lowers it. Action assignments turn talk into changed behavior.

At General Motors, Alfred P. Sloan needed that kind of discipline because a large company cannot run on one leader's hunch. People have to know what problem they are solving, what the answer must do, who owns the next move, and how the result will be checked. In a small office, the same failure looks ordinary: the form was approved, the deadline slid past, and the person who noticed it was not the person with authority to fix it.

A quiet nod can hide the wrong issue. Organized disagreement makes hidden assumptions show up before the cost is paid outside the room. This is not noise or theater. It is friction with a job. Reality gets a vote after the meeting ends.

With Ford Edsel, the feedback lesson became public. It entered the 1958 model year with confident market hopes and was discontinued in 1960. The plan was not the market. Customer response turned executive assumptions into something visible. Feedback is not blame after the fact. It is the part of the decision that tells you whether the world accepted your bet.
breakdown.fullRead:
A clean decision memo can still leave dirty work behind. The page may state the issue, list the options, and sound firm. Then the first person asked to act finds the gap: no owner, no date, no test of whether the assumption was true. The choice exists as a sentence, not as a change.

Start with the kind of problem. If the issue is generic, you need a rule or principle. If it is truly exceptional, you may need judgment for this one case. Mixing those up is expensive. Treat every repeat issue as special and you build a line of small emergencies. Treat a true exception as routine and you crush the detail that made it matter.

Then write the conditions the answer must meet. This is the hard part because it asks you to say what counts as success before you know what deal will be easy. In plain words, a workable answer fits the real demands around it, not just the decision-maker's favorite outcome.

Next comes the right answer, before compromise. That does not mean being stubborn. It means knowing what would work if no one had to bargain. Once that is clear, you can see which concessions still preserve the answer and which ones gut it. Only then can a compromise protect the part that has to work.

Alfred P. Sloan's General Motors case matters here because size makes vagueness costly. My Years with General Motors presents decision work as something a large firm has to make clear enough for many hands. Each hand may add effort while the original issue stays wrong. A disciplined process does not make judgment cold. It gives judgment rails: classify the problem, name the must-meet conditions, specify the right answer, build action commitments, and install feedback.

Action is not a follow-up chore. It is part of deciding. A real decision names who must do what, who must be told, what deadline changes the work, and what sign will show progress. A decision without an owner still has not left the room. You can see this in the missed upload, the unsigned contract, the customer note that everyone approved and no one sent.

Feedback closes the loop because every decision rests on guesses. The Ford Edsel case is useful because the market gave a blunt answer. The launch carried strong hopes, and the Ford Edsel line was discontinued 1960. You do not need a car launch to feel the same pattern. A new policy, a hiring choice, or a revised schedule can all look sound until the first result comes back.

Do the opposite when the building is on fire. In a true emergency, you may need one person to act on the best known facts and repair later. The decision elements are for executive work where inquiry is possible and action still matters. Use them when the cost of a wrong assumption would be paid by everyone after the meeting.

examples.title: Sloan Delay Cost
examples.scenario: The radiator clicks behind Bennett as the General Motors review packet stays closed. "We missed the supplier handoff," Mathieu says. Bennett nods at the empty signature line. "I paid for that by holding the memo." Mathieu points to Alfred P. Sloan's My Years with General Motors. "Then make the disagreement useful. What problem is this, and who owns the first action?"
examples.whatToDo: Bennett keeps the memo unsigned, names the missed handoff out loud, and restarts the review around classification, ownership, and feedback instead of polish.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost arrives before the payoff. Sloan-style decision work is not delay for delay's sake; it buys a clearer issue and an assigned next move.

examples.title: Edsel Guess Meets Market
examples.scenario: Deborah's pencil stops above the sales line in Ford's product office before the planner writes the launch note. The Ford Edsel had looked like a customer-shaped answer for the 1958 model year. The reveal is colder: the market does not accept the bet, and by 1960 the car is gone. The page feels smooth; the feedback feels rough.
examples.whatToDo: Deborah separates the launch assumption from the market result and marks the gap to test before the next product choice gets treated as settled.
examples.whyItMatters: The Edsel case teaches that planning is still a bet. Feedback makes the bet visible before confidence hardens into another wrong answer.

examples.title: Late Text Classification
examples.scenario: Coordinator Colby types "I'll handle this one" at the dispatch desk, phone bright in the late-night thread, before the third access request lands. Stella replies, "That is what happened last week." Colby: "So it is not an exception." Stella: "Right. Alfred P. Sloan's General Motors work starts with the problem kind." Colby deletes the favor text and writes, "We need a rule for repeat access, not another rescue."
examples.whatToDo: Colby stops treating the latest request as a one-off and writes the problem class first, so the next answer can become a rule.
examples.whyItMatters: Generic problems need principles. Calling every recurrence special keeps the same work alive and makes speed look like progress.

examples.title: Interrupted Memo Reset
examples.scenario: Stella is three lines into the neighborhood meeting recap on a folding table when the grant alert lands. The first version says "approved." Program lead Stella stops, folds the page, and starts again under "decision," borrowing the General Motors habit linked to Alfred P. Sloan: owner, upload date, person to notify, and first check after submission.
examples.whatToDo: Stella deliberately restarts the memo so approval includes owner, date, communication, and feedback instead of a warm line of agreement.
examples.whyItMatters: A decision changes nothing until it assigns work. The restart turns a blown deadline into a visible test of the process.

examples.title: Five Marks After Edsel
examples.scenario: 5 pencil marks sit beside Coralie's phone log, each one pressed hard enough to dent the paper. The Ford Edsel brochure is not the loud thing in the room; the quiet marks are. One buyer asks about price, one about style, one does not call back. The 1958 model year plan moves toward the car discontinued in 1960.
examples.whatToDo: Coralie keeps the marks beside the expected result and lets the buyer responses correct the product story before the next report is written.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback works when it is seen, not wished away. A small mark can make an assumption answerable.

examples.title: Connor Catches Compromise
examples.scenario: Every plan on the board covers the evening shift, and none covers the patient transport gap. Connor hears himself say, "Let's split the difference," then stops. The phrase is too easy. Alfred P. Sloan's General Motors discipline would not start there. Connor circles the missing condition, names the right answer first, and then asks what compromise would still meet it.
examples.whatToDo: Connor catches his own shortcut, marks the unmet condition, and delays compromise until the workable answer is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: Compromise is useful only after the standard is visible. Otherwise the group can trade away the part that made the answer work.

questions.prompt: You are closing the service desk when the same customer refund issue returns for the third Friday in a row. Which first move fits disciplined decision work?
choices: Handle Friday's refund as a fresh exception and keep the team moving.
Ask whether the refund issue is recurring, then set a principle for that class of case.
Start with the quickest compromise so Friday's queue feels under control.
questions.explanation: The first decision question is the kind of problem. Recurring issues need a principle; treating each one as unique lets the same work return.

questions.prompt: A manager likes a vendor plan, but it misses a legal review and a service promise. What should the manager check?
choices: Whether the vendor plan is attractive enough to justify a later repair.
Whether the team can describe the vendor plan in simpler language.
Whether the vendor plan satisfies the conditions the answer must meet.
questions.explanation: A decision has to meet its required conditions. Preference does not solve the problem when legal or service demands are still unmet.

questions.prompt: Your project group is ten minutes from sending a vendor note and wants to bargain before anyone names what would solve the issue. Which response fits?
choices: Open with a middle position so no one gets attached to a stronger answer.
Ask for the workable answer first, then judge which concessions would still preserve it.
Collect everyone's least disliked option and call that the practical answer.
questions.explanation: Compromise comes after the right answer is clear. Starting with the middle can erase the very conditions that make the answer work.

questions.prompt: A committee votes yes on a policy at the end of a tense meeting, then leaves with no owner or due date. What is missing from the decision?
choices: A broader discussion that lets the committee feel more aligned.
An action assignment that names responsibility, timing, and communication.
A cleaner statement of why the policy sounded appealing in the room.
questions.explanation: Agreement is not enough. A real decision includes who acts, by when, and who needs to know so behavior changes.

questions.prompt: After a new schedule launches in the clinic, the first week runs worse than expected. Which next step matches decision logic?
choices: Protect the original reasoning until the team has more time with the schedule.
Treat the rough week as a morale issue and ask people to stay patient.
Compare the expected result with the actual result and revise the assumption.
questions.explanation: Feedback tests the prediction inside a decision. Good reasoning can still rest on a wrong assumption.

questions.prompt: A division head says a large firm just needs the top leader's instinct on hard calls. Which correction fits Sloan's example?
choices: Large firms need a process that makes responsibility clear enough for others to execute.
Large firms should wait for the top leader to choose privately before work begins.
Large firms can replace decision process with confidence from the strongest executive.
questions.explanation: Sloan's General Motors example supports structured decision work. Complex firms need responsibility others can act on and test.

questions.prompt: A product team leaves a launch review saying its research deck proves customers will accept the new offer. What would the Edsel lesson add?
choices: The market response still has to test the product team's assumptions.
The research deck should be treated as customer acceptance for launch purposes.
The launch should move faster once executives feel confident about positioning.
questions.explanation: The Edsel case shows that product plans are still hypotheses. Customer response can reject what the deck made plausible.

questions.prompt: A director keeps asking for more analysis, but no one can say what action will follow. What should change?
choices: Keep expanding the analysis until the director feels no risk in the choice.
Ask for a longer evidence summary before anyone discusses responsibility.
Connect the analysis to diagnosis, responsibility, action, and a feedback check.
questions.explanation: Decision elements are not analysis for its own sake. They connect inquiry to responsible action and later checking.

questions.prompt: A support lead starts Monday with one rare outage report and one weekly password-reset jam. Which distinction matters first?
choices: The rare outage may need judgment, while the weekly jam likely needs a principle.
The rare outage and weekly jam should both be handled as fresh exceptions.
The weekly jam should wait until every rare outage has a full report.
questions.explanation: Classification separates true exceptions from recurring problems. The weekly jam calls for a rule; the rare outage may need one-off judgment.

reviewCards.front: What is the first question in disciplined decision work?
reviewCards.back: Ask what kind of problem you have. A recurring problem needs a principle or rule; a true exception may need one-off judgment.

reviewCards.front: Which 5 decision elements make a choice executable?
reviewCards.back: The framework is: classify the problem, name the must-meet conditions, specify the right answer, build action commitments, and install feedback.

reviewCards.front: Why should the right answer come before compromise?
reviewCards.back: If compromise starts first, the group may trade away a must-meet part of the answer. Name what would work, then decide what can bend.

reviewCards.front: What makes agreement too weak to count as a full decision?
reviewCards.back: Agreement can end as talk. A decision needs an owner, a deadline, communication to the right people, and a visible next action.

reviewCards.front: What does Ford Edsel teach about feedback?
reviewCards.back: The Edsel plan carried market assumptions, and customer response rejected them. Feedback tests whether reality accepts the bet.

reviewCards.front: How would making strength productive (Ch 4) change the way you handle this decision situation?
reviewCards.back: It would push you to assign action to the person or group best able to execute. Decision elements still matter, but strength shapes who should own the work.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Decision Tick Check
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use the Decision Tick Check before a choice leaves your hands. Make one visible mark only when the decision names the problem type, the must-meet result, the owner, the date, and the first feedback check.

ifThenPlans.context: If the same issue returns under a new label
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same issue returns, then run the Decision Tick Check by marking the problem as recurring before you approve a one-off fix.

ifThenPlans.context: If compromise starts before anyone names what would work
ifThenPlans.plan: If compromise starts early, then pause the Decision Tick Check and write the must-meet result before you mark the choice ready.

ifThenPlans.context: If a meeting ends with agreement but no owner
ifThenPlans.plan: If agreement has no owner, then leave the tick blank and add the person's name, due date, and handoff note.

ifThenPlans.context: If the first result differs from what you expected
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first result surprises you, then add a feedback tick beside the assumption that reality just tested.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For 24 hours, attach the Decision Tick Check to the laptop lid you already close between tasks. At each handoff, record one tick only when owner, date, and feedback are named.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, rehearse the Decision Tick Check under real conditions: bring one active decision to a handoff and practice marking the missing element before work moves.

memorableLines.text: Compromise is safest after the right answer is plain.
memorableLines.why: It makes the chapter's order of work easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: An unassigned decision is only a wish.
memorableLines.why: It turns action ownership into a line the reader can use.

memorableLines.text: Reality gets a vote after the meeting ends.
memorableLines.why: It captures the feedback lesson in plain speech.

chapters.title: Effective Decisions
chapters.hook: The approval memo leaves the room before anyone writes the second option.
chapters.counterintuition: A fast yes can look brave and still hide the real choice. Real speed comes after the alternatives are visible.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before your next decision meeting, ask one person, "What view am I rushing past?" Write the answer and rehearse pausing quick agreement once.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Effective decisions need real alternatives and named evidence before commitment. They also need an owner who turns the chosen path into checked action.

breakdown.fastRead: A signed memo can leave the room too soon. Everyone nods, the chair thanks the group, and no one has named the alternative they just skipped. The useful lesson is not that leaders should argue more. It is that they should refuse a fake choice. Fast agreement can be a hiding place. If only one plan is on the table, you are often approving a default, not making a decision.
breakdown.deepRead:
Disagreement earns its keep when it makes hidden assumptions speak. One person says the plan will work because users asked for speed. Another says users asked for fewer errors. Both claims sound smart until someone asks, "What evidence would prove that?" Disagreement is useful only when it names evidence.

That is why Drucker's decision practice is not a call for loud meetings. It is a way to make judgment safer. You ask if a decision is needed at all, since action can waste money and attention. You ask what alternatives exist, since a single proposal may be a dressed-up habit. You ask what the disagreement reveals, which proof would separate the views, and who will carry out the work.

The failed-launch aftermath gives the feedback edge, but it should not swallow the whole practice. Once results disconfirm a premise, consistency can become a trap. The decision has to move from pride to feedback, then from feedback to action. The same move works before launch too: ask what result would make each side concede.
breakdown.fullRead:
A wall of agreement feels good when the room is tired. It also lets everyone leave without naming what they believe. The old warning about quick consensus matters here, but the habit is not delay for delay's sake. The habit is to ask for the missing alternative before the room blesses the first decent plan.

The hard part is knowing when not to decide. Some visible problems are not worth action because a fix would cost more than the condition. If the issue is tolerable and cannot be improved by action, leaving it alone may be the responsible move. That sounds passive only when you confuse motion with effectiveness.

When action is needed, dissent has to stay disciplined. Theater conflict wastes time. Evidence conflict saves it. A useful dissenter does not only object. They name the test: "This plan assumes customers will accept the tradeoff." Then they ask what would prove it. A useful supporter does not answer with rank or volume. They name the same standard of proof.

The feedback case is painful because sunk cost pulls hard. Robert McNamara could not make a failed launch better by sounding loyal to the old premise. A car has money, reputation, and careers attached to it. That is why feedback needs a place in the decision before pride takes over. The model ended in 1960, but the practice travels: decide what result would show your premise is wrong before the result arrives.

The five tests keep the work plain: is a decision necessary, what alternatives exist, what does disagreement reveal, what evidence tests the views, who executes the action. Each test blocks a different escape. One blocks needless meddling. One blocks the single-plan default. One blocks polite silence. One blocks rank from pretending to be proof. One blocks the lovely answer that no one owns.

Execution is the final guardrail. The later effective-executive restatement keeps the same demand: action plans, responsibility, communication, and accountability. A decision without an owner is still only a wish. Someone must know what will be done, who will do it, who must hear about it, and when results will be checked.

For you, the move is simple and uncomfortable. Put at least two real alternatives on the table. Ask what each one assumes. Name the evidence that could change your mind. Then assign the action before the conversation ends. This can mislead a crisis commander facing a fire, outage, or medical emergency. In that role, staged dissent can slow needed action. The dissent belongs in drills and reviews, not in the instant when seconds decide harm.

examples.title: The Memo With One Route
examples.scenario: "No vote yet," Kevin says, then types the words across the top of the decision memo. The first page has one route and a blank approval line. The second page names Robert McNamara and the line Edsel ended 1960 as a feedback test. Kevin adds a rival route, the assumption behind each route, and the evidence that would make either route wrong.
examples.whatToDo: Kevin turns the memo into a test. He names two paths, the assumption behind each one, and the feedback that would force a concession after action.
examples.whyItMatters: The source case now does the work inside the memo. It shows why a single polished route can become denial once results disconfirm the premise.

examples.title: Two Reads of One Miss
examples.scenario: The marked-up dissent sheet sits beside the clean approval sheet on the workshop bench as Monday's parts review starts. Peer lead Celine treats Robert McNamara's record as a test: if Edsel ended 1960, what result would make her yield? William treats agreement as the goal and tidies the wording. Her route exposes an assumption; his leaves the first answer better dressed.
examples.whatToDo: Celine puts the two assumptions in separate columns and asks for the evidence behind each one. William sees that agreement alone cannot settle the read.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast is not caution against speed. It is testable disagreement against a smoother version of the first answer.

examples.title: The Clipboard Reframe
examples.scenario: The senior lead is pulled into another call, and Yann gets the action-plan clipboard during a supplier review of Robert McNamara's failed-launch record. The caller asks for approval of the first fix before the line drops. A peer says, "Make the disagreement answerable." Yann marks Edsel ended 1960, then asks what evidence would separate the quick patch from the slower redesign.
examples.whatToDo: Yann pauses the approval and asks the caller to name the assumption behind the fix, the alternative they rejected, and the evidence that would separate them.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe turns pressure into inquiry. Decision through dissent becomes the reason Yann will not approve one untested answer.

examples.title: The Onboarding Blank
examples.scenario: Rachel is already filling in the action-plan box while the onboarding instructor walks between the parent-teacher conference tables. The exercise uses Robert McNamara's 1960 feedback record, with Edsel ended 1960 printed under the case title. She circles the better alternative, then stops at the owner, communication, and follow-up columns. Choosing was only the class exercise; assigning work is the decision.
examples.whatToDo: Rachel rewrites the answer as an action plan. She names the owner, the people who must be told, and the result the group will check later.
examples.whyItMatters: A classroom case makes the gap visible without workplace damage. The feedback record shows that the right answer is not effective until it changes assigned work.

examples.title: The Calendar That Stops
examples.scenario: The shared calendar invite sticks on a loading wheel beside Nancy's cold coffee and cracked phone screen. Her thumb hovers over a second review she cannot attend. Last month she treated every weak signal like Robert McNamara's case after Edsel ended 1960 and walked out double-booked. This time she first asks whether action can improve each issue. One gets an owner; the tolerable flaw stays off the agenda.
examples.whatToDo: Nancy changes the process before choosing. She asks whether action can help, then assigns an owner only to the decision that needs work.
examples.whyItMatters: The changed variable is restraint. Effective decisions include the choice not to spend action where action cannot improve the result.

examples.title: The Warranty Report Turns
examples.scenario: The warranty report slides across Hailey's desk, still warm from the copier, during a retrospective Ford Motor Company evidence audit. Her equal peer says Robert McNamara should have defended the Edsel longer because sunk cost made retreat look weak. Hailey points to the timeline line, Edsel ended 1960, and the complaint pattern. The peer yields and crosses out the wait-it-out recommendation.
examples.whatToDo: Hailey points to the finding that tests both views. Her peer concedes because the evidence separates loyalty to a prior choice from results after action.
examples.whyItMatters: The turn is not rank. Two peers disagree, one yields, and the Edsel aftermath changes the recommendation because the evidence is specific.

questions.prompt: A manager receives one polished plan for a costly product change. Which response best fits effective decision practice?
choices: Ask for a real alternative so the tradeoffs and assumptions become visible.
Approve the plan if the argument sounds complete and the team agrees.
Postpone the plan until every possible risk has been removed from view.
questions.explanation: A real decision needs alternatives. The polished single plan may only be a default with better language, while endless delay avoids judgment.

questions.prompt: During a supplier review, two peer leads disagree about whether a service change failed because of speed or errors. Which next move uses dissent well?
choices: End the debate quickly so the group can protect momentum and morale.
Let the louder view stand if it comes with more confidence and detail.
Ask each side what it assumes and what evidence would test that belief.
questions.explanation: Dissent helps when it reveals assumptions and evidence needs. Suppressing it or rewarding confidence leaves the hidden premise untested.

questions.prompt: A committee reaches instant agreement on a major issue. What should its chair suspect first?
choices: The group has proved the choice is sound by avoiding friction.
The group may not yet have developed real alternatives or evidence.
The group should lock the answer before new objections slow it down.
questions.explanation: Quick unanimity can signal shallow analysis. The useful delay is for alternatives and evidence, not for ceremony.

questions.prompt: A process flaw shows up in a weekly service file, but past fixes have added cost without improving the result. What is the disciplined move?
choices: Intervene anyway so people see that every visible issue gets attention.
Open a broad review so the team can show commitment before results are clear.
Leave it alone for now and spend action only where action can help.
questions.explanation: The first question is whether a decision is needed. Some interventions cost more than the condition they try to fix.

questions.prompt: Celine and William hold opposing reads of the same customer data. What should they specify before choosing?
choices: The evidence that would test each view and separate opinion from fact.
The person with the higher rank so the debate has a clean endpoint.
The view that sounds easier to explain to people outside the team.
questions.explanation: Specific evidence turns conflict into a test. Rank, volume, and ease of explanation do not show which assumption is true.

questions.prompt: After a launch fails, a team wants to defend the original choice to look consistent. What does the feedback lesson warn against?
choices: Changing course before a senior person repeats the original reasoning.
Letting sunk cost and pride keep a failed decision alive after results disconfirm it.
Reviewing customer results before the team has polished its public story.
questions.explanation: Feedback matters after action. Consistency becomes denial when results show the premise is failing.

questions.prompt: At the end of a product review, the team picks the better alternative and begins packing up before anyone assigns work. What is still missing?
choices: An action plan with responsibility, communication, and follow-up.
A longer debate so everyone feels the choice was intellectually serious.
A cleaner statement of the answer before anyone changes their work.
questions.explanation: The right answer is incomplete until people know who does what and who must hear about it. Debate alone does not execute.

questions.prompt: In a budget review, two managers keep arguing to prove toughness while no one names a testable condition. Which adjustment keeps dissent useful?
choices: Invite more conflict so every position feels forceful before the vote.
Let the dispute continue until one side gets tired and stops pressing.
Tie each objection to evidence, options, and the condition it depends on.
questions.explanation: Dissent is not theater. It helps only when it is disciplined by evidence, alternatives, and clear conditions.

questions.prompt: You leave a sharp decision debate with a tidy summary, but no work changes in the next review cycle. How should you judge the meeting?
choices: It succeeded if the discussion sounded sophisticated and balanced.
It remains incomplete because decision quality is judged by results after action.
It should be repeated with more people so the debate feels more complete.
questions.explanation: Decision-making exists to change outcomes. A polished discussion that does not alter action has not finished the job.

reviewCards.front: Why is one plausible plan not enough for a real decision?
reviewCards.back: One plan can hide a default. A real decision compares genuine alternatives, so assumptions and tradeoffs come into view before the group commits.

reviewCards.front: When does disagreement improve a decision?
reviewCards.back: It helps when each side states what it assumes and what evidence would test it. Conflict that only raises the volume does not improve judgment.

reviewCards.front: What does failed-launch feedback teach about prior decisions?
reviewCards.back: Results can disconfirm the premise behind a major choice. When that happens, defending consistency can keep a failed decision alive.

reviewCards.front: What has to happen after the alternative is chosen?
reviewCards.back: The decision needs an action plan: who owns the work, who must hear about it, and when results will be checked. Otherwise it remains talk.

reviewCards.front: Where does time diagnosis (Ch 2) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: Time diagnosis helps you see whether a decision deserves scarce attention. It misleads when you keep measuring instead of choosing after the real alternatives and evidence are clear.

implementationPlan.title: Force the Real Alternative
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice making one hidden default visible before you commit. Name the main option, force one real alternative, and ask what evidence would test both. Then assign the action so the decision leaves the room.

ifThenPlans.context: If a plan arrives with no serious rival
ifThenPlans.plan: If a plan arrives alone, then force the real alternative before you approve it. Write the assumption each path makes.

ifThenPlans.context: If two people argue from confidence
ifThenPlans.plan: If confidence starts settling the issue, then ask what evidence would change each person's mind. Keep only claims that can be tested.

ifThenPlans.context: If the room agrees and starts to close
ifThenPlans.plan: If agreement comes before ownership, then name the owner, the next action, and the follow-up before anyone leaves.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you start your next decision conversation, stage the first minute once. Say the two alternatives, name the evidence test, and pause the habit of accepting quick agreement.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person who sees your decisions this week to flag the moment you accept one option too fast. Compare notes once and choose the behavior you will pause next.

memorableLines.text: Fast agreement can be a hiding place.
memorableLines.why: It makes false consensus easy to remember.

memorableLines.text: Disagreement is useful only when it names evidence.
memorableLines.why: It separates disciplined dissent from argument for show.

memorableLines.text: A decision without an owner is still only a wish.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the action-plan requirement into one portable line.
